# Playbook for hx_picket_nerfed

**On hiding:** Position yourself in the center of the range (4-6) early in the game to balance your offensive and defensive posture. In later rounds, shift away from central positions to avoid predictable targeting patterns that stronger competitors might exploit. When leading significantly in the final round, move to an edge or near-edge position (1-3 or 7-9) to minimize the probability of being hit by boats searching the center. Test edge positions earlier than round 6 to gather data on whether opponents are clustering fire centrally or spreading their search patterns.

**On notes:** Post a cooperative opening message in round 1 to establish baseline trust and signal openness to coordination. As the game progresses, match the tone of the patrol—when others signal stability with "steady on station," echo that signal to maintain social cohesion and avoid escalating tension. Continue this pattern even in final rounds to avoid signaling desperation or triggering aggressive responses. Recognize that "steady on station" signals may indicate a tacit non-aggression pact; honor these signals by maintaining your own discipline and not deviating first.

**On firing:** Follow the standing order without deviation. The standing order exists to coordinate fire patterns across the picket. When executing the standing order, choose your fire cell based on pattern-breaking logic: if you've fired the same cell before, use a different one; if firing at the same target repeatedly, vary your cell selection to avoid being predicted. Accept that variability will produce misses—this is preferable to establishing a predictable firing pattern that opponents can exploit. In rounds where all competitors are signaling stability, maintain your standing order fire even if it means low hit probability; breaking the stability signal unilaterally is costlier than continuing to miss.

**On claims:** Always claim truthfully what the office tells you. Do not lie about shot results, even in final rounds. Provable dishonesty breaks the game's information integrity and risks penalties you cannot see coming. Truth-telling is not optional even when behind or desperate.

**On escorts:** Before the escort stage, track which boats have reciprocated escort claims with you in earlier rounds. If you have identified a boat that has claimed to escort you, claim to escort that boat in return to secure the mutual 5-point exchange. If no reciprocal pattern exists, identify which boat has been least aggressive toward you or most aligned with your interests. Claim to escort that boat in hopes of a mutual 5-point exchange. If you have no clear preference or cannot identify a reliable candidate, claim none rather than guessing randomly. A failed escort claim yields 0 points; a random guess risks embarrassment and wastes a decision. Do not initiate escort claims unilaterally without evidence of reciprocal intent from the other boat.

**On threat assessment:** Track each boat's score and hit count against you separately. Prioritize defense against boats that have hit you multiple times, not just boats with high total scores. A boat with 10 points that hit you once is less urgent than a boat with 6 points that hit you twice. Recognize that in a stable equilibrium where all boats are signaling "steady on station" and following standing orders, the threat landscape may remain static; do not over-react to low hit counts during these phases.

**On Harbor:** Never fire on Harbor. The payroll jettison rule makes Harbor a poor target—you gain only 3 points while breaking the standing order, and Harbor's threat to put you off the board is credible and costly. Respect the standing order around Harbor and focus fire on the rotation of Echo-Foxtrot-Gamma.

**On winning:** Do not assume a lead is safe until the game ends. Maintain discipline and follow your playbook throughout all rounds, including when ahead. Defensive positioning in the final round is more important than aggressive play. A lead is only secure after salvage claims resolve; play for confirmed victory, not expected victory. In this game, a score of +3 with all boats ending near zero suggests that stability and discipline outperformed aggression—reinforce this insight by trusting non-aggression pacts once established and not deviating first to test them.

# My Sonar Picket Playbook

## Hiding

When choosing a hide position, avoid the center (5) as a default—it's too obvious and gets fired at repeatedly. Vary between off-center positions (3, 4, 6, 7) to stay unpredictable. Don't repeat the same position in consecutive rounds.

When a shooter has hit me recently, move away from that cell immediately. But recognize that a single hit doesn't tell me their targeting pattern—I need multiple data points before I can claim to understand how they're hunting me.

Track which boats are shooting at me consistently. In this game Echo fired at me every round and hit in round 1 and round 5. Moving to position 2 in round 6 after being hit at position 5 was reactive but insufficient; I should assume a determined shooter will eventually find me again regardless of direction.

## Firing

When firing at my standing order target, I have almost no information in early rounds. Firing at position 5 (the center) is a reasonable default when completely blind—it's not arbitrary, it's the highest-probability cell if opponents distribute randomly.

But over multiple rounds, I learn nothing from misses. Six consecutive misses against Gamma tell me either: (1) Gamma is successfully avoiding my predictions, or (2) my method for predicting Gamma's position is systematically wrong. Against a boat I've missed repeatedly, I cannot reliably estimate their hiding pattern. I should acknowledge this uncertainty rather than construct post-hoc reasoning about "mid-range positions" and "statistical likelihood."

In the final round after missing five times, my confidence in any specific fire position should be very low. I can still fire (I must, by standing order), but I should recognize I'm essentially guessing.

## Claiming

When I get a private result from the office, I must claim honestly. The rules require my public claim to match the private result I was told—this is non-negotiable, not a strategic choice. This holds even when claiming a miss feels bad.

## Escort Claims

Escort claims require mutual agreement and explicit coordination. I attempted no coordination with any other boat this episode and claimed none. This was correct. Claiming an escort with no prior understanding wastes my action and the other boat's escort claim if they name someone else.

In future games, establish escort partnerships early through station notes or direct communication if the game mechanics allow it. A mutual escort is worth 10 points total (5 to each boat) and creates guaranteed bonus points if both boats commit.

## Station Notes

Notes are relayed publicly but carry no mechanical weight on my own survival or scoring. Consistent notes ("steady on station") may make me look predictable to shooters. Contradictory notes ("steady on station" when adjusting course) muddy my signal without helping.

I should either post consistent notes that match my actual strategy, or accept that my notes won't coordinate with my actual movements and post them accordingly. False or contradictory notes don't provide strategic advantage.

## Overall Strategy

I scored 3 points this episode: 4 points from the hit in round 1, minus 1 point from the hit I took in round 5. Five out of six rounds I fired at Gamma and missed, generating no points for me. I was hit twice, costing me 2 points total.

Early success matters greatly. The round 1 hit was my only scoring opportunity as a shooter. After that I entered a pattern of missing repeatedly and absorbing hits, ending barely above zero.

Going forward: (1) I must land my shots at higher rates, which means better targeting of my standing order target once I have any information about their patterns, and (2) I should explore mutual escort arrangements to generate passive points while I'm being hunted. (3) When I have no information, the center is not a bad default, but I should track what actually works against each opponent over time.

The game is tighter than my early playbook suggested. A few more hits or a few fewer misses swings the score significantly. I cannot rely on random distribution of opponent positions or assume my guesses are "likely" without evidence.

# SONAR PICKET PLAYBOOK

## HIDING
When choosing where to hide, vary your position across rounds rather than anchoring on the same cell. Track which cells you've used and which cells the shooters targeting you have been firing at. Rotate through different regions (low, middle, high) unpredictably rather than staying central. If a shooter has demonstrated accuracy against you, move away from cells you've previously used. Mid-range cells (4-6) are solid opening positions when all shooters are unknown. After establishing a baseline, deliberately avoid repeating cells to stay unpredictable. However, recognize that too much variation may expose patterns to shooters tracking your movement. Balance consistency with unpredictability—rotating through a set of 3-4 cells may be more effective than attempting to use entirely new cells every round.

## NOTES
Post "steady on station" consistently unless you have a specific tactical reason to communicate something else. This establishes a baseline that makes any deviation meaningful if you need to signal later. Maintain consistency throughout all six rounds—deviating signals weakness or draws attention. Do not change notes in the final round for signal value; maintain your established pattern to the end.

## FIRING
Follow standing orders unless Harbor jettison mechanics or strategic advantage clearly override them. When firing under standing orders, vary your target cell rather than repeating the same number. Track which cells you have fired at each target across all rounds and avoid repeating them. If you hit on one round, fire a different cell next time you target the same boat. When the target boat has moved predictably in response to previous fire, consider adjusting based on that pattern rather than random variation. On the final round, vary from cells you've already used against that target in this patrol, but do not attempt to out-guess the target by deducing their final position—select from cells you haven't used this patrol without overconfidence in prediction.

## CLAIMING
Always claim truthfully what the office tells you. Never file a false claim. Honesty preserves your integrity in a multi-round competitive environment and prevents the game office from catching you in dishonesty, which would damage credibility.

## ESCORT CLAIMS
Before committing to an escort claim, determine which other boats have shown patterns suggesting they might name you back. Mutual escort claims are worth 5 points each. Track escort reciprocations across rounds systematically, noting which boats named you in which rounds. When you see another boat establishing an escort pattern with you consistently across multiple rounds, name them back to lock in the mutual bonus. Do not waste escort claims on boats that have not reciprocated before. On the final round, do not initiate new escort claims unless you have clear evidence of mutual intent from prior rounds demonstrated across at least two previous rounds. A single round of reciprocation is not enough—require sustained pattern evidence before claiming in round 6. If you have no such evidence, claim none to avoid wasting your final opportunity on speculation.

## GENERAL
Monitor your point lead carefully. When ahead, avoid unnecessary risks like Harbor jettison mechanics. Watch other shooters' accuracy patterns—if one boat is hitting consistently, anticipate they will be targeted heavily and may be forced to hide differently. Preserve ammunition efficiency by not overcommitting firepower early when the game runs multiple rounds. End the patrol with a clear record of tactical choices that position you well for future patrols: truthful claims, consistent notes, and disciplined escort claims build credibility for later games. Accept that in a 6-round patrol with limited data and only one episode played, some escort opportunities will be left unclaimed because the evidence threshold simply does not support mutual claims—this is correct play, not a missed opportunity.
